items.title: Remarkable Biosynthetic Diversity in the Bionectriaceae: Uncovering the genomic basis of antipathogen bioactivity of cacao fungal endophytes Clonostachys rosea and Waltergamsia zeylanica.
items.blurb: Cacao (Theobroma cacao) production in tropical countries is threatened by fungal diseases caused by Moniliophthora roreri and M. perniciosa. Two cacao pod endophytes from Bionectriaceae, Clonostachys rosea TCF417 and Waltergamsia zeylanica TCF400, exhibit growth antagonism towards M. roreri; however, the genetic basis underlying the bioactivity of these strains has not been addressed. Here, we aimed to identify biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) potentially associated with the antifungal bioactivity of these two strains and performed a comparative analysis with 30 publicly available Bionectriaceae genomes using BiG-SCAPE. Whole-genome sequencing using Oxford Nanopore and Illumina technologies, resulted in assemblies of 52.9 Mb (C. rosea TCF417) and 31 Mb (W. zeylanica TCF400). Genome annotation was conducted using Funannotate, and secondary metabolite BGCs were predicted using antiSMASH. The two cacao endophytes harbored 92 BGCs (C. rosea: 67; W. zeylanica: 25), indicating remarkable biosynthetic diversity. Across all 32 genomes, 1,523 BGC-containing regions were identified, most belonging to T1PKS clusters. Network-based clustering revealed 209 gene cluster families (GCFs), of which 52 corresponded to previously characterized BGCs. Conserved BGCs for antifungal compounds, including sorbicillinoids and verticillins, were identified in cacao endophytes and across Bionectriaceae. Additionally, an antifungal assay conducted here demonstrated that verticillin D from C. rosea TCF417 exhibited growth inhibition of plant pathogens Moniliophthora roreri and Mycena citricolor. With about 75% of unassigned GCFs, our results reveal a largely untapped biosynthetic repertoire in the Bionectriaceae and identify verticillin D as a candidate contributor to the antagonism of C. rosea against plant pathogens.

items.title: High-Resolution Spatial Transcriptomics Reveals Millimeter-Scale Malignant Territories and Immune Exclusion patterns in Human Salivary Gland Adenoid Cystic Carcinoma
items.blurb: Background/Objectives: Adenoid cystic carcinoma (ACC) of the salivary gland (SGACC) is a rare malignancy with frequent late recurrence and limited response to systemic and immune therapies. Bulk and single-cell sequencing do not preserve tissue architecture, so the spatial organization of its MYB-driven myoepithelial and luminal tumor cells, stroma, and immune cells remains poorly defined. This study aimed to map the SGACC tumor microenvironment at near-cellular resolution. Methods: Visium HD based spatial transcriptomics was performed on four SGACC tissue sections from three patients with tubulo-cribriform tumor form in stage III - IV. Bins of 10 x 10 {micro}m were annotated and deconvolved with cell2location using an integrated single-cell reference of 119,189 cells from 20 donors. Pseudobulk differential expression, spatial autocorrelation, potency and spatial trajectory inference, permutation-based territory analysis, Hotspot module detection, and marker-based immune profiling were applied. Results: MYB-expressing luminal (LECs-MYB) and myoepithelial (MECs-MYB) epithelial cells occupied 55.7% of bins on average. The MECs-MYB to LECs-MYB ratio increased from the nest interior toward the tumor edge, where cancer-associated fibroblasts rose sharply. Potency and trajectory analyses placed MECs-MYB upstream of LECs-MYB. Malignant states formed territories of up to 38.0 mm2 that persisted over 1.5 mm in three sections and contained spatially restricted programs. Hypoxic stressed territories also showed mTORC1, unfolded protein response, and cell-cycle programs. T/NK, myeloid, MHC class I and II, and plasma cell signatures were 1.4- to 5.7-fold higher in stroma than in tumor nests, whereas VTCN1 (B7-H4) was the only B7 family ligand enriched within nests. Conclusions: SGACC shows an ordered arrangement of malignant lineages, millimeter-scale malignant territories, MHC class - I and II enriched stroma, and immune-excluded nests enriched for B7-H4. These features provide evidence to be validated in larger cohorts with protein-level and clinical data.

items.title: Bryostatin-1 exploits a developmental signaling vulnerability in MEF2D-rearranged B-cell precursor acute lymphoblastic leukemia
items.blurb: MEF2D-rearranged (MEF2D-r) B-cell precursor acute lymphoblastic leukemia (BCP-ALL) is a rare molecular subtype associated with high-risk clinical features and frequent relapse and characterized by a distinctive pre-B-cell developmental state and dependence on pre-B-cell receptor (pre-BCR) signaling. Despite these distinctive biological features, MEF2D-r BCP-ALL lacks subtype-directed therapy. Here, we identify a pharmacologically actionable vulnerability to the diacylglycerol (DAG) mimetic bryostatin-1 (Bryo-1). Across 93 BCP-ALL cell lines, MEF2D-r models were enriched for Bryo-1 sensitivity, although responses varied within the subtype and extended to selected non-MEF2D models. Sensitive cells responded at low-nanomolar concentrations with rapid ERK activation followed by loss of pre-BCR-associated components, reduced proliferation, caspase activation and cell death. Pharmacological MEK inhibition markedly attenuated Bryo-1-induced loss of viability, supporting a functional involvement of MEK-ERK signaling. Time-resolved phosphoproteomic and proteomic analyses further revealed coordinated activation of DAG-responsive signaling and subsequent remodeling of the precursor B-cell state. Bryo-1 also altered immunotherapy-relevant surface antigens, including CD19, CD20 and CD22, as part of this broader cell-state transition. Importantly, low-nanomolar activity was reproduced ex vivo in MEF2D-r patient-derived xenograft cells. Together, these findings support pharmacological activation of a negative-selection-like developmental checkpoint as a potential therapeutic strategy in responsive MEF2D-r BCP-ALL and provide a framework for biomarker-guided functional patient selection.

items.title: EPIC2: integrating single-cell chromatin accessibility with human genetics to identify trait-relevant cell types
items.blurb: Summary: EPIC2 is a computational and statistical framework for prioritizing trait-relevant cellular contexts by integrating genome-wide association study (GWAS) summary statistics with single-cell chromatin accessibility data. It accounts for linkage disequilibrium when testing for association between GWAS association strength and cell-type-specific chromatin accessibility at both SNP and regulatory-peak resolutions. The resulting P-values are combined using the Cauchy combination test. Availability and Implementation: The core workflow is implemented in R, with source code, vignettes, and reproducible test data freely available at https://github.com/LingxuanZ/EPIC2. Supplementary Information: Supplementary material accompanies this preprint.

items.title: Xist deletion in T cells protects against influenza-induced lung injury
items.blurb: Sex differences in antiviral immunity are well established, yet the contribution of X-Chromosome Inactivation (XCI) to T cell responses during infection is unknown. Here, we identify an unexpected role for Xist RNA in shaping T cell immunity and pulmonary injury following influenza infection. We show that the inactive X chromosome (Xi) in pulmonary CD4+ and CD8+ T cells undergoes dynamic epigenetic remodeling, with limited Xist RNA localization, differential enrichment of H3K27me3 and H2AK119Ub modifications, and activation-dependent XCI escape of immune-related genes, including Il2rg and Cxcr3. Remarkably, T cell-specific Xist deletion protects female mice from influenza-induced weight loss and pulmonary pathology despite comparable early viral burdens. Transcriptomic profiling reveals increased expression of X-linked escape genes and antiviral and interferon-responsive genes, particularly in CD8+ T cells. Furthermore, Xist-deficient CD4+ and CD8+ antigen-experienced (CD44+CD11a+) T cells exhibit increased biallelic Cxcr3 expression, elevated pulmonary Cxcr3 protein levels, and enhanced IFN-{gamma} and TNF responses following ex vivo stimulation. Together, our findings reveal a previously unrecognized role for Xist RNA in regulating female antiviral T cell responses and demonstrate that enhanced T cell effector potential can accompany reduced infection-associated pulmonary injury.

items.title: Structural correlates of disease-associated CTSC variants in Papillon-Lefevre syndrome
items.blurb: Objective: To quantify structural features of disease-associated CTSC missense substitutions and evaluate a structural rule for research prioritization in Papillon-Lefevre syndrome. Design: We compared 16 ClinVar pathogenic or likely pathogenic missense substitutions with 234 recurrent gnomAD substitutions in the mature cathepsin C structure (PDB 1K3B). An expanded exploratory analysis included 35 further literature-indexed substitutions. We audited the documentation used to date the historical holdout and compared AlphaGenome splice scores with a consequence-only baseline. Results: Median predicted destabilization was 2.209 versus 0.763 kcal/mol (AUC 0.764, 95% CI 0.612-0.897). Catalytic proximity was observed in 4/16 versus 9/234. The expanded comparison gave AUC 0.740. Sixteen of 31 substitutions in the historical post-2015 subset had references dated through 2015. For noncoding variants, AlphaGenome splice scores and the consequence-only baseline both obtained AUC 1.000 on 12 positive and 105 negative ClinVar records. Conclusions: Predicted destabilization was associated with ClinVar label status in this dataset. The literature chronology and noncoding consequence composition limit claims of predictive validation.

items.title: Minimal eukaryotic DNA polymerase zeta/Rev1 GC-pair mutasome
items.blurb: In eukaryotes, translesion DNA synthesis (TLS) enables replication across DNA lesions, difficult DNA structures, and during replicative stress. While TLS prevents replication fork collapse, it is inherently mutagenic and requires tight regulation to prevent global mutation rates increase. Here, we show that elevated DNA polymerase pol {zeta}/Rev1 promotes spontaneous mutagenesis during replication. The five subunits of pol zeta complex (pol zeta5) are the catalytic subunit Rev3, the TLS polymerase Rev1, a dimer of accessory protein Rev7, the Pol31 and Pol32 subunits shared with replicative pol delta. Pol31 and Pol32 bind the Fe-S-containing C-terminal domain (CTD) of Rev3, which serves as a major assembly hub. We found that overproduction of pol zeta5, but not four-subunit pol zeta4 lacking Rev1 or Rev1 alone, increases spontaneous mutation rates by up to 20-fold, indicating that pol zeta5 can access undamaged DNA during replication and compete with replicative DNA polymerases. This mutator effect is independent of PCNA ubiquitylation. augments by hydroxyurea and synergizes with DNA mismatch repair defects. Overproduction of a pol zeta5 complex containing CTD-truncated Rev3 is also mutagenic, demonstrating that active TLS complexes can assemble and function without the canonical CTD interaction hub. Both complexes predominantly generate CG-to-GC transversions, a mutational pattern that resembles several COSMIC cancer mutational signatures. Inactivating Rev3 catalytic activity abolishes mutagenesis, whereas loss of Rev1 catalytic activity substantially reduces mutation rates and eliminates CG-to-GC transversions, identifying Rev1 as the primary cause of the observed mutation pattern. The findings reveal previously unrecognized mechanisms of pol zeta-dependent mutagenesis with broad implications for cellular evolution and cancer development

items.title: Chemolithoautotrophic acidophile phenotyping by measuring metabolic byproduct formation in microplates
items.blurb: Chemolithoautotrophic acidophiles can support several low-pH biotechnologies, but their phenotyping remains limited by throughput and inconsistent methods. This study used an assay to monitor metabolic byproduct formation using absorbance indicators in static, oxic cultures in 96-well microplates. In abiotic experiments, ferric iron and/or pH measurements from 51 microplates containing simulant solutions span total iron concentrations of 0-1 M, pH 0.3-7.0, and incubation temperatures of 4-75 {degrees}C. Of these, 30 microplates tested different UV-transparency and gas-permeable membrane configurations. Another 12 microplates tested indicator compatibility with growth media containing ferrous iron and (in)soluble sulfur substrates. Biological experiments measured 438 microplates containing Acidithiobacillus ferrooxidans ATCC 23270, Acidithiobacillus thiooxidans ATCC 19377, or Leptospirillum ferriphilum DSM 14647 with chemical additives across 1,400 concentration conditions, yielding 142,038 time-course points, including abiotic controls. Measurements of apparent substrate oxidation and/or growth from 96 culture tubes and 99 shake flasks provide context for microplate observations. The miniaturized assay and this dataset may be useful for microbiology, (critical-mineral) biotechnology development, and synthetic biology.

items.title: Distinct innate immune states associate with divergent serological outcomes after syphilis treatment
items.blurb: The global resurgence of syphilis poses a major public health challenge, even in the era of effective antibiotic therapy. Following treatment, some patients achieve seroreversion, whereas others remain serofast with persistent nontreponemal antibody reactivity. Although nontreponemal antibody titers guide clinical follow-up, it remains unclear how closely they reflect the resolution of inflammation and recovery of immune function. We integrated single-cell transcriptomics, immunophenotyping in clinical samples, and functional assays to characterize circulating monocytes and natural killer (NK) cells across seroreversion and low- and high-titer serofast states, and further examined the impact of HIV coinfection. CD14+ monocytes retained inflammatory and CD163-associated scavenging programs after seroreversion, whereas serofast patients showed additional IFN-STAT1 activation in this subset. NK cells from serofast patients exhibited reduced JUN expression and impaired degranulation. JNK inhibition reduced the magnitude and altered the kinetics of NK cell degranulation, IFN-{gamma} production, and amphiregulin (AREG) induction. Among low-titer serofast patients, HIV coinfection was associated with higher mitochondrial complex I gene expression and partially restored NK cell degranulation compared with patients with syphilis alone. Complex I inhibition also reduced NK cell degranulation. These findings suggest that seroreversion does not necessarily indicate immune normalization and identify post-treatment immune alterations not fully captured by conventional serological monitoring, providing a rationale for investigating cellular immune markers as complementary measures of recovery after syphilis treatment.

items.title: Single-base 5mC and 5hmC profiling identifies a dynamic 5hmC-to-5mC transition at gene bodies and transcription end sites during neuronal differentiation of mouse embryonic stem cells.
items.blurb: 5-methylcytosine (5mC) and 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC) are genome-wide epigenetic modifications involved in chromatin organization and transcriptional regulation. Although Enzymatic Methyl-seq (EM-seq) can enable the combined profiling of 5mC and 5hmC, Enzymatic 5hmC-seq (E5hmC-seq) can provide selective profiling of 5hmC at single-base resolution. In this context, we systematically validated E5hmC-seq using diverse genomic DNA samples. Next, we integrated E5hmC-seq with EM-seq to distinguish between 5mC and 5hmC landscapes during neuronal differentiation of mouse embryonic stem cells. First, we observed dynamic remodeling of both modifications throughout differentiation, with pronounced changes during the transition from embryoid bodies (EBs) to neural progenitor cells (NPCs), characterized by a global decrease in 5hmC accompanied by an increase in 5mC. Subsequently, differentially hydroxymethylated regions (DhMRs) exhibiting 5hmC depletion frequently showed a concurrent increase in 5mC, whereas regions gaining 5hmC displayed an opposing trend, reflecting the genome-wide relationship. Mapping these modifications to transcriptional profiles revealed an association between cytosine modification dynamics and gene expression, where transcriptional downregulation correlated with 5hmC depletion with concomitant 5mC enrichment. In summary, combined mapping of EM-seq and E5hmC-seq can decipher the dynamic interplay between 5mC and 5hmC at single-base resolution and provide insights into the relationships among cytosine modification dynamics, genomic context and transcriptional regulation during differentiation.

items.title: Unexpected Long Range Actions of AAV8
items.blurb: Adeno-associated virus vectors (AAVs) have broad utility in neuroscience. A variety of features, such as titer, capsid, enhancers and promoters, coding and non-coding elements, can be utilized to pursue diverse experimental ends. The net effects of titer and capsid have been used experimentally to pursue retrograde and anterograde studies, such as through the monosynaptic spread of high-titer AAV1. The literature on AAV8 is conflicting, with evidence for and against its long-range action outside of the infected starter population. Using the mouse corticopontocerebellar tract, we report that AAV8, when used at high titers, can be associated with long range recombination outside of the starter population. This phenomenon depended upon the viral titer and was influenced by the presence of other experimental injections. Surprisingly, separate injections of high-titer AAV8 recombinase and recombinase-reporter AAV8s gave rise to recombination across long distances in populations not known to be monosynaptically connected. Given the possibility of long range and emergent effects, we suggest that investigators empirically determine titer, capsid, and injection designs that reduce false positives and/or indirect effects.

items.title: Astrocyte-secreted Cathepsin D regulates hippocampal memory through extracellular matrix remodeling
items.blurb: Astrocytes contribute to hippocampal cognitive functions, but how astrocyte-derived factors regulate memory formation remains unclear. Here, we identify astrocyte-secreted Cathepsin D (CtsD) as a regulator of hippocampal learning and memory. Proteomic profiling of hippocampal astrocytes upon learning identified candidates predicted to be secreted, among which we focused on CtsD, whose extracellular brain functions are unknown. Neutralizing extracellular CtsD or astrocyte-selective CtsD knockdown (aCtsD-KD) impaired hippocampal long term potentiation (LTP) and memory acquisition, suggesting an extracellular role for astrocytic CtsD. In aCtsD-KD mice, these deficits were accompanied by alterations in excitatory transmission and synaptic structures. aCtsD-KD also caused abnormal extracellular matrix (ECM) accumulation, and its partial digestion by chondroitinase ABC rescued the memory deficit, indicating that astrocytic CtsD-dependent ECM degradation contributes to hippocampal memory. Together, our findings suggest a CtsD-dependent astrocyte-matrix-synapse axis regulating hippocampal memory.

items.title: Macrophage signaling history constrains subsequent transcriptional responses to cytokine stimulation
items.blurb: Macrophages perform a wide array of distinct and crucial functions, and therefore tightly regulate their responses to external stimuli. These cells must integrate sequential signals over time to mount an appropriate response to their immunological niche. How prior cytokine stimulation shares macrophage responses to a subsequent stimulus remains poorly understood, yet has important implications for pathogen clearance as well as tissue repair and homeostasis. Here, we systematically characterize transcriptional responses to sequential cytokine stimulation in primary human macrophages, as well as demonstrate the effect of interactions with bacterial pathogens on macrophage transcriptional responses and plasticity. We find that prior stimulation history constrains subsequent transcriptional responses in a stimulus-specific and asymmetric manner. Across the cytokines we tested, we observe that IFN{beta} is a dominant regulator of subsequent responses to other cytokines. We observe that this plasticity restriction is concentration dependent, rapidly established, and persists after cytokine removal. Additionally, we show that endogenous IFN{beta} produced during infection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis restricts subsequent cytokine responses in a manner that is dependent on the activity of the bacterial secretion system ESX-1. Taken together, these findings establish a hierarchical model of macrophage responses to cytokines that depends on cytokine identity and order.

items.title: RADSuite: Improving Species-Level Identification in Microbiome Research
items.blurb: In the last twenty years, the microbiome has become a central focus of biomedical research, with amplicon sequencing of the 16S rRNA gene considered the industry standard for taxon identification of prokaryotes due to its cost-effectiveness. However, common target regions in 16S amplicons often do not uniquely distinguish closely related species, restricting many analyses to the genus level. Additionally, curated databases such as NCBI's 16S curated database often do not contain all intragenomic variants of the 16S gene and lack annotation of the 16S genomic composition and gene structure. To address these limitations, our team created RADSuite, a collection of tools which includes a more robust database of 16S gene copies (RADlib), an application that identifies which V regions will allow for species level identification (RADx), and a step-by-step guide for how to integrate RADlib within existing metagenomic profiling software tools. Here we demonstrate the utility of using RADSuite as a guide for designing 16S amplicon sequencing experiments. For example, RADx can be used to recommend 16S components that enable species-level resolution for most microbes of interest, even when industry-standard default amplicon choices (V3/V4) are insufficient. These findings suggest that targeted variable region selection is critical for reliable species identification. As researchers use RADSuite to improve the quality of their experiments, we anticipate improved experimental accuracy in fields of microbiome research from human health to environmental conservation.

items.title: MicroBioAgent: an AI agent for automated microbiome analysis
items.blurb: Microbiome data analysis demands customized workflows tailored to specific biological questions, sequencing modalities, and data properties. However, constructing and executing these workflows requires navigating heterogeneous software dependencies, reference databases, and multi-step parameter tuning. Here, we present MicroBioAgent, an autonomous, domain-specific agent framework that translates high-level biological queries into executable, study-specific pipelines across 16S rRNA amplicon, reference-based shotgun, and de novo assembly-based metagenomics. Rather than relying on static pipeline templates, MicroBioAgent employs a closed-loop execution architecture: it dynamically selects and runs bioinformatics tools within user-controlled environments while iteratively inspecting intermediate outputs to adapt downstream analytical decisions. Furthermore, to address the long-running nature of metagenomic computation, we introduce an asynchronous background task-management mechanism that reduces LLM token consumption by over 50% while enabling real-time plan adjustment and automated workflow resumption. We systematically evaluated MicroBioAgent across three benchmarks of increasing complexity: (1) paired amplicon and shotgun profiling of tomato rhizosphere microbiomes, (2) taxonomic and functional profiling coupled with machine-learning classification in a colorectal cancer cohort, and (3) de novo metagenomic assembly, metagenome-assembled genome (MAG) binning, and metabolic pathway reconstruction in a polyethylene degradation study. Across all benchmarks, MicroBioAgent faithfully recapitulated the primary biological findings of the original studies, exhibiting high analytical concordance despite expected tool- and database-dependent variations. In systematic robustness evaluations across 27 independent runs spanning three backbone large language models and three prompt-complexity tiers, MicroBioAgent achieved a 98.8% task completion rate and yielded highly reproducible diversity and differential-abundance estimates. MicroBioAgent establishes a scalable, adaptive paradigm for end-to-end computational microbiome research.

items.title: Dual mRNA delivery corrects physical and biochemical deficits in a mouse model of hepatic onset trifunctional protein deficiency
items.blurb: Mitochondrial trifunctional protein deficiency (TFP-D) is a rare, life threatening long-chain fatty acid oxidation disorder caused by variants in either the HADHA or HADHB subunits, leading to toxic metabolite accumulation and systemic energy deficiency. Current dietary management strategies are only partially effective and fail to prevent long term morbidity and mortality. Here, we developed a lipid nanoparticle (LNP) mediated mRNA replacement strategy to restore TFP function in a moderate severity TFP-D mouse model by delivering both Hadha and Hadhb mRNA. In cultured TFP-D mouse fibroblasts, dual mRNA delivery, but not single subunit replacement, rescued long-chain fatty acid oxidation and revealed a dominant negative effect exerted by the endogenous M404K variant Hadhb. In vivo, intravenous administration of dual mRNA-LNPs restored hepatic TFP expression, reduced circulating long-chain acylcarnitines, and improved physiological performance in aged TFP-D mice. Notably, intravenous delivery of dual mRNA LNPs significantly rescued cold tolerance test (CTT) performance by up to 71.6% compared to untreated and healthy controls. Together, these findings establish dual subunit LNP-mRNA delivery as a promising therapeutic strategy for TFP-D and support its potential applicability to other long-chain fatty acid oxidation disorders.

items.title: Training background shapes the exercise-induced extracellular vesicle proteome to acute exercise with partial overlap with cold exposure in humans
items.blurb: Aim: Exercise and cold exposure changes circulating extracellular vesicle (EV) and modifies their molecular cargo. However, it remains unclear whether the acute exercise-induced EV proteome response is uniform or shaped by long-term training background, and to what extent it overlaps with the response to cold exposure. We therefore performed an exploratory proteomics study in humans with distinct training phenotypes and compared exercise-induced protein changes with an independent cold exposure dataset. Methods: Serum samples were collected before and immediately after a maximal bicycle ramp test from untrained sedentary controls, endurance-trained athletes, natural bodybuilders, and sprinters. For cold exposure studies, serum samples were collected before, immediately after, and 30 minutes after an ice bath (8-12 degree Celsius) for 5 minutes. EVs were isolated by differential ultracentrifugation and characterized using electron microscopy and nanoparticle tracking analysis. EV proteomics was analyzed by LC-MS/MS. Differential relative protein abundance was assessed within each training group. Shared significance, concordant directionality, functional enrichment, and comparison with the independent cold-water immersion cohort were analysed. Results: Acute exercise altered the serum EV-enriched proteome in all training groups, but the response differed substantially between groups. Sprinters showed the largest number of altered proteins, whereas endurance athletes, bodybuilders, and sedentary controls displayed more selective responses. Few proteins were significantly altered across multiple groups, although a broader set showed concordant directional changes, indicating a limited shared response superimposed on training background-specific remodeling. Functional enrichment highlighted extracellular vesicle and extracellular compartment signatures together with immune, adhesion, trafficking, and stress-response pathways. Cold exposure also induced time-dependent remodeling of the serum EV-enriched proteome, with the largest number of altered proteins observed 30 minutes after exposure. Comparison of the immediate cold response with exercise revealed partial directional overlap, particularly with endurance exercise, but also clear stimulus-specific differences. Conclusion: Our results suggest that changes in the EV proteome profiling after acute exercise are highly dependent on the training background in humans. Rather than revealing a single universal EV protein signature, acute exercise produced group-specific EV proteome remodeling together with a smaller layer of shared directional trends. The comparison with cold exposure supports the concept that acute physiological stressors can remodel concomitant circulating EV protein profiles, while also producing stimulus-specific signatures.

items.title: Deciphering the role of adenosine-related genes in regulating smooth muscle cell phenotypic switch in coronary heart disease via single-cell RNA sequencing
items.blurb: Background: Coronary heart disease (CHD) is closely associated with dysregulated lipid metabolism, inflammation, and impaired adenosine signaling. However, the contribution of adenosine-related genes (ARGs) and their relationship with the immune microenvironment remain unclear. Methods: Public transcriptomic datasets were integrated with curated ARGs. Differential expression analysis and weighted gene co-expression network analysis identified candidate genes, and XGBoost, support vector machine-recursive feature elimination, and Boruta were used to select diagnostic features. Gene set enrichment, immune infiltration, regulatory-network, and single-cell RNA-sequencing analyses were performed, followed by reverse transcription-quantitative polymerase chain reaction validation. Results: We identified 4,884 differentially expressed genes and 243 ARG-associated module genes, yielding 231 candidate genes. DYRK2 and SIGIRR were prioritized as key genes and were consistently downregulated in bulk CHD datasets, including the validation cohort. A two-gene nomogram showed strong diagnostic performance. Functional analyses linked both genes to mitochondrial dysfunction and innate immune regulation, while immune profiling indicated reduced adaptive immune populations and enhanced myeloid-associated inflammation. Single-cell analysis identified smooth muscle cells as a key compartment with altered DYRK2 and SIGIRR expression along pseudotime trajectories and remodeling of vascular endothelial growth factor and pleiotrophin signaling. Reverse transcription-quantitative polymerase chain reaction in clinical samples (n = 5 per group) supported the bioinformatic expression trends (P < 0.05). Conclusions: DYRK2 and SIGIRR emerged as key adenosine-related genes associated with immune-metabolic imbalance and smooth muscle cell dysfunction in CHD. These findings provide a basis for further mechanistic and translational validation.

items.title: Beta-Myosin inhibition in skeletal muscle: Impact of Mavacamten on the diaphragm
items.blurb: The diaphragm, a primary respiratory muscle, contains nearly equal proportions of slow, Type-1 and fast, Type-II muscle fibers. Muscle fiber types - classified based on their shortening velocities and force generation abilities - are largely determined by distinct myosin II isoforms. Mavacamten (MAVA), a small molecule inhibitor of beta-cardiac myosin ATPase, is currently used for the treatment of obstructive Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy (HOCM). Notably, beta-myosin heavy chain (beta-MyHC) is not restricted to the ventricular myocardium but is also expressed in slow fibers, raising concerns about off-target effects of therapy used to treat cardiomyopathic conditions. Given that nearly 50 % of the fibers express beta-MyHC in the diaphragm, we hypothesize that Mava may affect diaphragm muscle activity. Using an in vitro motility assay, we investigated the effects of Mava on native myosins isolated from rabbit diaphragm muscle and measured the velocity of actin and regulated thin filaments. Mava caused a dose-dependent decrease in myosin-driven actin filament velocity, with an apparent IC50 of 1350 nM. Importantly, this inhibition was reversible upon drug washout, indicating a non-permanent modulatory effect. To determine the drugs fiber-type specificity, we tested pure slow- and fast-myosin isoforms from the slow-twitch M. soleus and fast-twitch M. psoas. Both isoforms were inhibited by Mava, but slow myosin exhibited nearly 20-fold greater sensitivity than fast myosin, suggesting a potentially stronger impact on slow fibers. Interestingly, the slow myosin isoform showed even higher sensitivity to Mava than beta-cardiac myosin. Further mechanistic analysis distinguished two modes of action: (i) promotion of the OFF state of myosin, likely reducing a pool of active motors interacting with actin filaments, and (ii) modulation of the actomyosin biochemical cycle. Altogether, given the diaphragms reliance on both fiber types for sustained respiratory function, this off-target effect may impair respiratory performance in patients undergoing therapy, underscoring the need for respiratory function monitoring. The studies have direct implications for understanding the modulation of myosin function under physiological and pathophysiological conditions, as well as following pharmacological interventions.

items.title: Nuclear quantum effects on ion permeation through the open transient receptor potential melastatin 7 pore: A continuum-electrostatics estimate
items.blurb: We estimate how nuclear delocalization affects magnesium and calcium release from occupied wells in the naltriben-open pore of transient receptor potential melastatin 7 (TRPM7). We compare the equilibrium distributions of sodium, magnesium, and calcium in the same open structure and fixed continuum field. Thermal quantum states extend over nearby positions, so the ion can sample more than one local environment. For the divalent ions, the model combines a Gaussian test charge in the nonlinear Poisson--Boltzmann potential, spatial dielectric self-energy, and the free-energy cost of restricting a correlated first hydration shell. The hydration shell comprises the water molecules that directly coordinate the ion. In a constriction, the wall can block access to some of these water sites. The classical and quantum calculations use the same insertion energy, pore geometry, and axial diffusivity. The leading Wigner--Kirkwood correction for a smooth ion energy $U_i$ away from the wall is $ell_i^2left[nabla^2 U_i-frac{beta}{2}|nabla U_i|^2right]$, up to an additive constant, with $ell_i^2=frac{betahbar^2}{12m_i}$ for ion mass $m_i$ and inverse thermal energy $beta$. The length $ell_i$ is about $0.02,text{AA}$ at $310,text{K}$. At the point-ion magnesium basin, the refined centerline self-energy reaches $430,text{meV}$. Steric constraints also restrict water coordination at the $1.43,text{AA}$ constriction. At $310,text{K}$ in the primary extended dielectric box, the deepest wells for magnesium and calcium lie at $22.75$ and $11.00,text{AA}$, respectively. The quantum changes in mean passage time toward the intracellular and extracellular interfaces are $0.68%$ and $-0.66%$ for magnesium and $-0.10%$ and $16.12%$ for calcium. Calcium starts on the intracellular side of the constriction and must cross it to reach the extracellular interface. The preferred magnesium site is already on the extracellular side. A change in the dielectric boundary for magnesium or the ligand penalty for calcium can move the deepest well across the constriction and reverse the extracellular response. For comparison, the circular point-ion estimate for magnesium changes from $-37.4%$ and $-34.5%$ to $-8.9%$ and $-8.6%$ with a $0.5,text{AA}$ wall inset. In the circular reference, the largest local correction occurs at the intracellular widening and depends on near-wall access and axial sampling. Its influence on escape from the occupied well is small. In a separate screened two-ion benchmark, classical repulsion changes escape barriers by tens to hundreds of meV. Isotope substitution tests the mass dependence at fixed charge and chemistry. Together, the results show how pore geometry, dielectric response, and water coordination determine which local quantum corrections affect directional release.

items.title: Interspecies differences in lamina cribrosa fiber composition and architecture might arise from differences in optic nerve head size and mechanical constraints
items.blurb: The lamina cribrosa (LC) is a complex network of fibers that plays an important mechanical role in protecting optic nerve axons as they exit the eye. Both the architecture and composition of the LC network varies throughout animal species. However, the function of these differences between species is unknown. We hypothesize that this variety in LC architecture and composition is a result of species-specific adaptations to the mechanical constraints present in each species' optic nerve head. To test this hypothesis, we developed a novel optimization framework to systematically derive optimal LC fiber architecture and composition under different mechanical constraints. We then compared predicted LC architectures to instant polarized light microscopy images of actual human, tree shrew, monkey, cow, pig, and rat LCs. Distinct features from the various LCs were replicated by varying the mechanical constraints, consistent with our hypothesis. The wheel-and-spoke architecture of the tree shrew LC was captured with angularly symmetric loading conditions. Non-radial fibers like those found in monkey and human LCs were captured by adding horizontal eye rotation tractions. The softer glial LC of the rat and stiffer collagenous LC of larger species were replicated by a two-material extension of the model. To our knowledge, these are the first results that systematically show how interspecies differences in LC architecture and composition can arise from mechanical constraints and size. This work can result in better interpretation of animal models and provide a point of comparison for changes in LC architecture under pathological conditions such as glaucoma.

items.title: How can we explain psychosomatic illnesses?
items.blurb:
Emotions play a significant part in physical symptoms – but not in the way people often imagine

When Diego started seeing bright flashing lights in his field of vision and felt his legs go weak, he thought he knew immediately what was happening. His mother had a stroke in her 60s, and although Diego was active and (unlike his mother) didn’t smoke, he had always expected that the same would happen to him. So it was a huge relief to be told – after seeing a stroke specialist and having a brain scan – that he had not had a stroke at all. Unfortunately the relief was short-lived. The visual disturbances and the weakness were real and debilitating. If this wasn’t a stroke, what was it?

Some illnesses aren’t caused by disease or damage, but arise when the coordinated functioning of the body goes awry. In a percentage of these cases a person’s psychological health is an important element in their symptoms. Intuitively this seems mysterious. We are accustomed to thinking about physical symptoms as being caused by physical events; viruses, inflammation, bleeding. How can something as intangible as a thought have any impact on something as physical as a leg? How can the mind make us ill?

items.title: ‘Hell dorm’: Florida prisoners testify about 119F heat indexes and walls that sweat
items.blurb:
Temperatures in a concrete facility contributed to one man’s death after he struggled to breathe, prisoners allege

On Tuesday afternoon Dwayne Wilson, 69, a thin Black man dressed in a light gray prison uniform, testified about the stifling heat he experienced in the Dade correctional institute, a concrete state prison south of Miami, Florida, without air conditioning. He removed his glasses and wiped his eyes as he spoke. “It was so hot,” he said, his voice catching. “It’s so hot sometimes you have to put water on the floor just to try to keep cool.”

Wilson said he’s housed in the H dorms, a T-shaped building with one-to-two-person cells, nicknamed “hell dorm” by prisoners because its concrete walls radiate heat absorbed from the sun. The plaintiff’s law firm, the Florida Justice Institute, convinced a judge to allow 31 sensors to be temporarily installed throughout the prison during the summer of 2025. They recorded temperature and humidity levels that Stefano Shiavon, a professor of civil and environmental engineering with expertise in thermal comfort, used to calculate the heat index. He found it to be above 88F (31C) 97% of the time, with the highest heat indexes often recorded at night, including one reading in the H dorm dayroom equivalent to 119F (48C) at 10pm one July day last year. “The walls sweat,” Wilson said. “It’s miserable in the cell at night because, again, it’s so hot. No air comes to the bed we sleep at and the bed is soaked in sweat.”

items.title: ‘I don’t blame any woman for being sucked in’: how the wellness industry is cynically exploiting menopause
items.blurb:
Where women see hot flushes and brain fog, pharmaceutical companies see dollar signs. But are products like lion’s mane mushrooms or even magnets for knickers really helping them? Or is it all just a big capitalist con?

‘Tequila?” says a woman brightly, proffering a pink plastic shot glass. It’s barely 10.30 on a Saturday morning, and my perimenopause wellness journey is not going entirely as expected. We are standing in a neon-lit London conference centre amid the hubbub of Pause Live, billed as the UK’s biggest annual women’s health and menopause event and essentially a consumer fair for those in midlife. All around me, women are sampling free squirts of menthol lotion (supposed to cool hot flushes) and paper thimblefuls of slightly grainy, sweet latte made with powdered Peruvian maca root instead of coffee.

The tequila, it turns out, is a gift from the sponsors, with no miracle ingredients beyond alcohol. But stalls offer everything from neck creams to pelvic-floor trainers, mindfulness journals and hairpieces for disguising thinning locks, plus herbal supplements in every conceivable edible form: chocolate truffles, ginger shots, mushroom coffee. (Fungi are big news in the menopause wellness world, often touted as an answer to brain fog. Though at best the scientific jury is still out, Ocado searches for lion’s mane mushrooms more than quadrupled after an episode of Clarkson’s Farm in which Jeremy Clarkson’s partner, Lisa Hogan, persuaded him to grow them to make supplements, claiming that “everyone who’s anyone” is on them.)

items.title: A truism for our political leaders: until work again involves respect and decent levels of pay, this crisis will continue | John Harris
items.blurb:
Last week’s Milburn review contained telling phrases, but the core problem is not Neets: it’s what capitalism as we know it has done to employment

Everyday pride and contentment. That’s what work should give us. In 15-plus years of speaking to ordinary people and politicians about this country’s serial woes and crises, one thing has revealed itself to me time and time again: the mess of cant, contradictions and tensions in our national understanding of work. Indeed, the higher up the hierarchies of power and influence any conversation about work goes, the more one vitally important subject seems to fall away: what paid employment actually is or ought to be.

All of this is reflective of a very British kind of amnesia. Of course poorly rewarded, unreliable jobs have always been part of our economy – and in the past a focus of fierce social conflict. But well within living memory a combination of the power of trade unions and the collective social conscience built into the postwar consensus resulted in an economy and labour market that now seem almost inconceivable. For sure they were scattered with restrictive practices and base prejudice: fathers securing jobs for their sons, people from minorities being excluded from work not just by people in management but by their fellow workers, and a great deal of sexism. But one of the tragedies of Labour’s 18 long years of exile from power and the climactic defeat of organised labour in the miners’ strike was the fact that they opened the way for the wholesale reinvention of work and watershed developments that we seem to be only just waking up to.

items.title: César Azpilicueta: ‘At Chelsea a draw was a catastrophe – if you can’t perform, you’re out’
items.blurb:
Former defender reflects on his record-breaking longevity, kicking Eden Hazard in training, and life after retirement

César Azpilicueta looks well. César Azpilicueta always looks well – “ah, Captain Handsome,” one Chelsea fan says when told who’s turning up – but today especially, smiling in the sunshine. Strolling in, he eases into an easier chair, golf course spreading out beyond the terrace, west of Madrid, and orders a detox almost as green. It is nearly 20 years since he played his first game and a few months since he played his last, training kit replaced by bermudas, loafers and a polo, a picture of relaxation. So what’s it like not being a footballer? “Well, different,” he says. Then he laughs, which he does a lot.

It is not a laugh-your-head-off laugh, more a chuckle, a giggle, as if amused at everything he did. And for all the self-deprecation, the lack of triumphalism, he did everything. Now, at 37, it’s not the same, although there remains much to do, Azpilicueta as understated and quietly busy as ever: “square,” he calls himself. He’s completed an MBA, a sports directorship diploma and there are media offers, a life to live. Matches to play still: against his kids the needle is never far away, he says. And although he hasn’t found a seven-a-side team yet he will.

items.title: Aston Villa held at home as dogged Sunderland battle for Régis Le Bris
items.blurb:
For Aston Villa, a painful stalemate at home to Sunderland, but for Régis Le Bris and his players, this was another triumph of sorts. The raw numbers spoke volumes of Villa’s struggles against a defence that backed themselves to keep Unai Emery’s side at bay. All but one of Villa’s seven shots on target came from outside the visitors’ box and the one inside it, courtesy of Ian Maatsen, was forgettable. Owing to a summer of change, injuries and Emery resting John McGinn with Tuesday’s game at Galatasaray in mind, Maatsen, incredibly, was the sole survivor in the Villa starting XI from when these sides played out a 4-3 classic seven months ago.

Villa were too predictable, short of a spark, someone to unpick an organised back line. Johan Manzambi, Emi Buendía and Alysson all flattered to deceive on an afternoon when Ibrahim Mbaye and McGinn arrived from the bench. Alejandro Garnacho, however, was not involved in Villa’s matchday squad for the second successive match and the Chelsea loanee has played just 38 minutes in the Premier League this campaign. Tammy Abraham, the match-winner in April, was also left out and a January move looks likely.

items.title: Yemen Market and Trade Bulletin October 2026 - Issued on 21st November 2026
items.blurb:
Country: Yemen
Source: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations

Please refer to the attached file.

SHORT-TERM OUTLOOK AND IMPLICATIONS ON FOOD SECURITY:

While Yemen’s acute food security crisis—with roughly 18.7 million people (over half the population) facing acute food insecurity (IPC Phase 3 or worse)—remains driven by heavy import dependency, rising food and fuel prices, severe humanitarian funding deficits, and climate and rainfall shocks, conditions have deteriorated sharply amid renewed frontline conflict and regional spillover effects. Since July 2026—and intensifying in September around Ta’iz, along the western coast, and across southern flashpoints—escalating hostilities and displacement have placed severe strain on overstretched services and existing displaced populations, while access constraints and road/maritime disruptions have slowed trade flows, pushed up freight and fuel costs, and restricted humanitarian reach. These compounding shocks—aggravated by funding shortfalls and climate stress—are eroding household purchasing power and driving acute deprivation, with millions facing IPC Phase 3 or worse conditions and localized emergency/catastrophe risks in late 2026.

KEY HIGHLIGHTS:

  • EXCHANGE RATES: Currency stability continued. The exchange rate remained broadly stable in GoY-controlled areas, trading 4% below its level a year earlier and 8% below the three-year average—indicating a firmer Yemeni rial against both benchmarks.
  • FOOD PRICES: Key staples became more expensive. In GoY-controlled areas, flour and basmati rice prices rose by 7.4% and 6.3% month-on-month, while sunflower oil and beans increased by 3.3% and 3.6%, respectively.
  • MINIMUM FOOD BASKET (MFB): Food-basket costs increased. Minimum Food Basket (MFB) costs in GoY-controlled areas rose 2% month-on-month from August, standing 7% above September 2025 levels and 2% above the three-year average—further squeezing household food affordability.
  • FOOD AND FUEL IMPORTS: Grain arrivals in GoY areas declined sharply. Recorded wheat and flour imports fell by 1.5% nationally and by 42.5% through southern ports. Recorded petrol and diesel imports also decreased by 9.9%; however, the absence of northern records limits the interpretation of this trend.
  • FUEL PRICES: Official diesel eased but remained elevated. Diesel prices fell by 4.5% month-on-month while petrol remained broadly stable; however, both fuels stayed substantially above last year's levels and their three-year averages.
  • TERMS OF TRADE (ToT): Flour purchasing power weakened. The Government of Yemen’s casual labor-to-flour terms of trade declined by 7.2% month-on-month and 23.1% year-on-year. Agricultural and composite livestock-to-flour ratios also decreased.
  • CASUAL LABOR WAGE RATES: Daily rates barely adjusted. In GoY-controlled areas, casual wages slipped 0.4% month-on-month and remained 9.7% below year-ago levels, while agricultural wages edged up by 0.4%.
  • LIVESTOCK PRICES: Modest recovery offered limited relief. Goat and local sheep prices increased month-on-month by 1.6% and 2.4%, respectively, but remained below their levels from the previous year.

Villagers planted food for elephants, mapped their migration routes, and worked to create safer corridors for these gentle giants. Today, over 300 elephants pass through Hatikhuli every year, offering a powerful example of what can happen when communities choose understanding over conflict. items.title: College Team Creates a Whole New Spring to Double Drinking Water Supply in an Uttarakhand Village
items.blurb: In the mountain villages of Uttarakhand's Tehri Garhwal district, the amount of drinking water available to families can change dramatically with the seasons. Many households depend on natural springs fed by rainfall and water stored underground. As summer approaches and these springs begin to lose their flow, families are left managing increasingly limited supplies. For residents of Unchaun village in the Kirtinagar block, seasonal water shortages have been a concern. And their experience is shared by several other villages in the region. A 2023–24 annual report by Himmotthan Society documents a similar challenge in Sabli village, also in Tehri Garhwal. A survey conducted in June 2022 found that all 52 households depended on a local spring for drinking water during summer because piped supplies were either unreliable or unavailable. The spring's flow dropped from 30 litres per minute during the monsoon to just five litres per minute in May and June. Over four summer months, the village faced an estimated water deficit of 14 lakh litres. These figures offer a glimpse into how difficult the dry months can be for communities that depend on mountain springs. Now, researchers at the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Roorkee have developed a new spring in Unchaun, using scientific research to locate and bring underground water to the surface. According to a Ministry of Education announcement on 2 November 2026, the intervention has increased daily drinking-water availability from approximately 500 litres to 1,000 litres or more during the lean season. The interesting part is how the researchers identified where this water could be found. Where does a Himalayan spring get its water? The intervention is part of IIT Roorkee's project, Rejuvenation of Drying Springs in Takoli Gad Catchment of Tehri District, Uttarakhand . Led by Professor Abhayanand Singh Maurya from the Department of Earth Sciences, the project draws on two studies examining how Himalayan springs are replenished and how water moves through underground rock formations. The research was conducted in the Takoli Gad watershed, a 143-square-kilometre area in the Lesser Himalayas, within the Alaknanda River basin. The first study, published in the Hydrological Sciences Journal in October 2026, examined where spring water comes from and how it travels underground. Researchers studied rainfall patterns and used measurements of different forms of hydrogen and oxygen, including radioactive tritium, to trace the movement and replenishment of groundwater. Their findings revealed just how important the monsoon is for sustaining Himalayan springs. Approximately 82% of spring-water recharge in the studied watershed comes from monsoon rainfall. Winter precipitation contributes around 10%, while pre-monsoon rainfall accounts for the remaining 8%. In simpler terms, much of the water that eventually emerges from these springs enters the ground during the rainy season. Some of it remains stored underground, helping sustain water sources even months after the monsoon has ended. The researchers also examined how long water stays underground before emerging through springs. A second study, published in Applied Geochemistry in 2026, looked at how the rocks beneath the hills influence the chemical composition of spring water. It found that interactions between water and carbonate rocks play an important role, alongside seasonal rainfall, soil carbon dioxide and human activities. Together, these studies helped researchers understand how springs are replenished, what influences their water quality and where groundwater might be available. IIT Roorkee Research Doubles Water Availability in a Himalayan Village During Lean Season Turning scientific research into tangible impact, IIT Roorkee has developed a new spring in Unchaun village, Tehri Garhwal, Uttarakhand, increasing lean-season drinking-water availability from approximately 500 litres to 1,000 litres or more per day. Led by Prof. Abhayanand Singh Maurya, Department of Earth Sciences, the initiative combines scientific understanding of spring-recharge dynamics, groundwater processes and geophysical investigations with targeted recharge interventions to address seasonal water scarcity. Supported by Namami Gange, National Mission for Clean Ganga, Ministry of Jal Shakti, Government of India, the project demonstrates the potential of research-driven solutions to strengthen rural water security. Building on two research studies published in Hydrological Sciences Journal and Applied Geochemistry, the initiative highlights how scientific insights can translate into effective, locally relevant interventions for Himalayan communities. With Prof. K. K. Pant, Director, IIT Roorkee, emphasising research with societal impact, this effort reinforces the Institute's commitment to advancing sustainable solutions for critical environmental and water challenges. #IITRoorkee #WaterSecurity #HimalayanWater #NamamiGange #SpringRejuvenation #GroundwaterRecharge #ResearchForImpact #SustainableDevelopment @iitroorkee @Director_IITR @cleanganganmcg @DoWRRDGR_MoJS — IIT Roorkee (@iitroorkee) November 2, 2026 How the team brought underground water to the surface The researchers began by studying the rock formations beneath the hillside to identify areas capable of holding and carrying groundwater. Once they located promising water-bearing layers, they estimated their depth and extent. The team then designed trenches along the uphill slope. These trenches help slow rainwater flowing downhill, allowing more of it to seep into the soil and replenish underground water reserves. At a suitable water-bearing layer, the researchers created a controlled opening that allowed groundwater to emerge at the surface. This resulted in a new spring near the road leading to Chandrabadni Temple. The reported result is an increase of at least 500 litres of drinking water available daily during the lean season, a potentially important improvement for households that depend on local sources. Springs are among the most important sources of freshwater for communities across the Indian Himalayan region. Photograph: (Representational image-Jeremy Graham / Alamy) Could this help other Himalayan villages? Across the Himalayas, springs are an important source of drinking water, particularly in remote villages where other supplies can be unreliable. The Unchaun project offers one way of addressing seasonal shortages: studying how water moves beneath a particular hillside before deciding where to intervene. As Professor Maurya explained in the Ministry of Education release, “Understanding the source, movement and seasonal behaviour of spring water is essential to addressing water scarcity.” The project has shown promising early results, but its long-term success will depend on whether the new spring continues to provide water through changing seasons. Researchers will need to monitor its flow and water quality over time. For now, the intervention offers a potentially useful approach for other Himalayan villages facing similar shortages, while showing how research into something as familiar as rainwater can help address everyday water needs. items.title: ‘I Left a US Tech Career To Turn My Father’s Surplus Amla Into 25+ Products for 4000 Customers’
items.blurb: By the time the amla ripened at her father's farm in Iduvai, Tamil Nadu, there was more fruit than the family could consume or sell fresh. Around 25 trees were bearing heavily, and the harvest would not wait for buyers. For Kalaiselvi, a former software professional who had spent nearly a decade working in the United States, the surplus presented a question: Could the fruit be preserved and sold long after its season had passed? That question led to Aruvi Eco Organics, which now makes more than 25 products, from amla jaggery candy and dried fruit to herbal teas and leaf powders. Kalaiselvi estimates that processing helps the farm use nearly 60 percent of its suitable surplus produce, depending on the season. The venture also supports a six-member core team. “My father laid the foundation for our venture through his commitment to organic farming. My contribution has been to build on that legacy by trying out how we can process the produce, reduce avoidable losses, and make natural food products available to more people,” she tells The Better India . A return to her father’s farm Kalaiselvi grew up in an agricultural family in Iduvai. In 1999, her father, Subramaniam, began developing their ancestral land into what the family called Aruvi Farm, growing amla, sapota, mango and guava without chemical pesticides. Kalaiselvi estimates that processing helps the farm use nearly 60 percent of its suitable surplus produce, depending on the season. She remembers planting seeds during childhood summer holidays at her aunt's house. Her parents encouraged their daughters to study while keeping a connection to the land, but her own ambitions took her towards computers. After studying computer science and engineering at Kongu Engineering College, she worked in Chennai before moving to the US in 2006 to join her husband. Her IT career included stints at AT&T, Frontier Communications, Verizon and Highmark in Pittsburgh, where she worked as an application developer. In March 2015, the couple returned to India with their two young children. Her father-in-law was facing serious health issues, and they wanted to be closer to their parents and raise their children here. They settled in Chennai, where Kalaiselvi spent time helping the children adjust, then worked in recruitment and scientific publishing. She also started Kana Bags, an initiative making cloth bags as alternatives to plastic ones. When the pandemic disrupted that venture in 2020, with the children's classes moving online, the family began spending more time on the farm in Iduvai. Kalaiselvi saw firsthand the labour behind her father's harvest, and the problem that accompanied it. “I got a closer understanding of the effort behind cultivation and the challenges that come with storing and managing the harvest,” she recalls. The amla crop was particularly abundant. Even with buyers, fresh fruit had a limited window in which it could be sold. “Instead of looking at the surplus just as produce that could not be sold in time, I started seeing it as an opportunity to create value-added products,” she says. From a dryer in the living room to a food business Her father showed her a newspaper article on value addition, and she joined an online session offered by Tamil Nadu Agricultural University. Sasikumar's connection with the farm goes back further. He joined as a helper in January 2008 and gradually learnt planting, tractor operation, and electrical repairs. She began experimenting with drying amla and sapota, initially using a coir-tray dryer that cost about Rs 28,000. She installed it in her Chennai living room; her father sent fruit from the farm by overnight parcel twice a week. The early batches taught her that turning fruit into a product was more complicated than finding a recipe. She sought training at the ICAR-Krishi Vigyan Kendra in Tirupur, Tamil Nadu Agricultural University in Coimbatore and the National Institute of Food Technology Entrepreneurship and Management. Over roughly two years, she learnt about handling produce, moisture, food safety, packaging and shelf life. Guidance from a food technologist at the Krishi Vigyan Kendra also helped her understand which ideas could be made consistently and sold commercially. “A recipe may work once, but achieving the same taste, texture, and quality consistently across batches is a completely different challenge,” she says. “I had to experiment repeatedly, understand how ingredients behave during processing, and learn how factors such as drying, moisture, and storage affect the final product.” Training introduced her to around 25 possible products. Rather than produce everything, she and her father chose ideas that suited what grew on the farm and their preference for avoiding artificial colours, flavours and synthetic preservatives. In 2021, the family also tested selling sapota and mango directly to consumers . Their first order was for sapota, but the pilot reinforced how difficult it could be to find buyers before fruit spoiled. By April 2022, the family had moved permanently to Iduvai. Working alongside Subramaniam, Kalaiselvi made the experiments more systematic, and Aruvi began commercial sales towards the end of that year. A June 2023 video about her journey on the agricultural YouTube channel Tamizhan Agri helped introduce the products to a wider audience. What goes into making 25+ natural food products Aruvi's catalogue has grown to more than 25 products, including over a dozen made with amla. Alongside jaggery-sweetened amla candy are dried mango and sapota, moringa and curry leaf powders, herbal infusions and products made from jamun seeds. “I never set out to build a large product line. Each new addition came from identifying an opportunity to make better use of what we grew and finding ways to meet customer needs,” Kalaiselvi says. Over roughly two years, she learnt about handling produce, moisture, food safety, packaging and shelf life. The choices extend to packaging. Aruvi uses cotton bags for its herbal dip teas instead of nylon mesh. Produce is harvested, sorted and cleaned, with damaged portions removed. Depending on the product, the team cuts or deseeds fruit before drying or further processing. The team checks each batch for appearance, texture, aroma and moisture, then packages and stores it carefully. Samples are sent to a NABL-accredited laboratory at Tamil Nadu Agricultural University in Coimbatore for nutritional and quality assessment. Working without synthetic preservatives makes consistent processing and storage especially important. The family farm supplies most ingredients, with additional produce sourced from farmers and producers around Tirupur when needed. For Kalaiselvi, this is where her previous career has proved useful. The discipline of software development, she says, helped her approach new recipes through testing, documentation and problem-solving, even as she learnt the practicalities of working with seasonal crops. The people behind every packet As orders grew, Aruvi's work created roles beyond the family. Six people now make up its core team across farming, processing, packaging and operations. For some, the change has meant a dependable income; for others, a chance to use or develop new skills. Mahalakshmi, 41, joined in February 2024 after spotting a banner advertising work at the farm gate. A single mother raising two children, she had previously worked in tailoring and papad-making units. She began by collecting leaves and fruit, then learnt food processing from Kalaiselvi. Today she helps maintain the workspace, stitches cotton tea bags and operates the amla-deseeding machine. “I did not have much knowledge of food processing or how farm produce could be turned into different products,” she says. “At Aruvi Eco, I got the opportunity to learn new skills under the guidance of Kalaiselvi ma’am.” Earning Rs 5,000 a week has made a difference at home. Her daughter is in college and her teenage son is studying for a diploma. Where she once sometimes turned to relatives for help with education expenses, she says she can now meet more of those costs herself. “Today, I feel proud that I can earn and take care of many of my family’s needs myself,” she says. “Apart from being my only source of income, this job is an opportunity to build a better future for my children.” Ramar and his wife Uma joined in March 2026. They had moved to Tirupur in search of work and were employed at a stitching unit when they saw an advertisement for jobs at Aruvi. Ramar has a degree in agriculture and now handles planting, watering, pruning and tree care under Subramaniam's guidance. Uma works with fruit and flowers in processing. He earns Rs 6,000 a week and she earns Rs 4,000. Together, they support three children and their elderly parents. The family farm supplies most ingredients, with additional produce sourced from farmers and producers around Tirupur when needed. “I was happy to get an opportunity to return to agriculture, while my wife could contribute to food processing,” Ramar says. Sasikumar's connection with the farm goes back further . He joined as a helper in January 2008 and gradually learnt planting, tractor operation, maintenance, plumbing and electrical repairs. Today he manages much of the daily farm work and coordinates packing and dispatch. His wife, Sumithra, stitches cotton tea bags from home using a machine supplied by Kalaiselvi. When a customer complained that a tea bag floated instead of staying immersed, Sasikumar suggested adding two stitches. The adjustment worked and became part of the process. “I never imagined that a job I started as a helper would allow me to learn so many skills and take on such responsibilities,” he says. “I feel that my experience matters and that I can contribute ideas that make a real difference to the business.” A longer life for the fruit, and a new beginning after 40 Kalaiselvi estimates that nearly 60 percent of suitable surplus produce that might previously have gone unused is now processed. It is an approximate, seasonal figure, rather than a fixed share of everything the farm grows. Processing also means the family has more ways to earn from fruit instead of relying only on fresh-produce prices during a short harvest window. By December 2024, Aruvi had reached more than 4,000 customers and recorded around 450 orders in one month. Sales have come through its website, Amazon and WhatsApp, while exhibitions, farmers' markets and food events have helped people across India discover the products. Some ingredients are sourced from neighbouring producers, giving the business opportunities to connect with other growers too. Kalaiselvi saw firsthand the labour behind her father's harvest, and the problem that accompanied it. Growth comes with its own demands. Availability changes with each season, small batches take planning, and products without synthetic preservatives need careful hygiene and moisture control. Kalaiselvi has had to learn about equipment, investment, pricing and winning customer trust. “Perhaps the biggest challenge was changing our own mindset. From thinking like farmers who wanted to avoid wastage to thinking like entrepreneurs who had to create a product, a brand, and a market around that surplus,” she says. She hopes to improve processing capacity and quality checks, work with more local farmers, reach retailers and business customers, and create more jobs. But she keeps returning to the person who made the journey possible: her father, who began tending the ancestral land long before she imagined working on it herself. “Today, the farm means much more to me than a piece of ancestral land. It is a part of my family’s history, a teacher, a workplace, and the foundation of Aruvi Eco,” she says. She was over 40 when she began learning food processing. Starting again meant being a beginner after years in an established career, a possibility she hopes other women will consider too. Mahalakshmi, 41, joined in February 2024 after spotting a banner advertising work at the farm gate. “I started this journey in a completely new field after 40, and there were many things I had to learn from scratch,” she says. “That experience has given me a strong belief that women, and anyone who feels it is ‘too late’ to begin something new, should not let age stop them.” What began as a question about unsold amla has become a way to carry forward her father's work, give the harvest more time to find a buyer and build livelihoods around the farm she once visited on holidays. An unpopular school with empty places is far more likely to be asked to merge, or close, than one that is sought after by parents.
